summary: This unit teaches you to make the foundations of good cooking: stocks (white, brown, fish and vegetable), the classical sauces (béchamel, velouté, espagnole, tomato and hollandaise), and clear and thick soups, including Jamaican favourites such as red peas soup, pepperpot, fish tea and pumpkin soup. You will also learn to thicken, season, strain, hold, cool, store and reheat them safely.

blocks.p: Stocks, sauces and soups sit under almost everything a kitchen sends out: a gravy for a roast, a cheese sauce for a vegetable dish, a pot of red peas soup on a Saturday. A cook who can make them well gives every dish more flavour, uses bones and trimmings that would otherwise be waste, and keeps costs down. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees.

They are also among the **riskiest foods in the kitchen**. A big pot of hot liquid is heavy and can scald. It cools slowly, and the warm liquid is the perfect place for bacteria to grow. A sauce or a soup that has been held too long, cooled badly or reheated more than once can make guests ill. So this unit is about safe handling and food safety as much as about flavour and technique.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's training kitchen. In the practical tasks you make stocks and sauces and several soups. The assessor watches your safety, hygiene, tasting, timing and clean-up as well as the finished dish.

blocks.note: Scalds from hot stock, soup and sauces are among the commonest serious kitchen injuries. For a scald, cool the area under cool running water for at least 10 minutes, take off anything tight (rings, watch), do not burst blisters or use butter or toothpaste, and get medical help for a bad one. Report it and write it in the accident book.

For sauces and small soups. A heavy base spreads the heat so that the sauce does not catch and burn.
Whisks make a smooth sauce and mix a roux; wooden spoons do not conduct heat; ladles move liquid.
A flat spoon with holes, for lifting scum and fat from the top.
To strain stock so that it is clear. A muslin cloth gives the finest result, for example for consommé.
A pan of hot (not boiling) water in which a container of sauce is kept warm for service.
To purée soups and make a smooth sauce. Always follow the maker's safety instructions.

blocks.h: Mise en place and standard recipes

blocks.p: **Mise en place** (French for 'putting in place') means having everything ready before you start: ingredients washed, cut, weighed and measured; equipment and containers ready; the area clean. A **standard recipe** is the written recipe that gives exact ingredients, amounts and method, so that the dish tastes, looks and costs the same each time and every guest gets a fair portion.

ul: Read the recipe through to the end before you start.
Weigh and measure; do not guess.
Use clean, dry measuring jugs and spoons, and clean scales.
Clean as you go: a clear, tidy bench is a safe one.

blocks.p: To change a recipe for more or fewer portions, divide the amount in the recipe by the number of portions it makes, then multiply by the number of portions you need. Do the sum twice.

head: Example
Working
rows: A soup recipe makes 8 portions and needs 1.2 kg of pumpkin. How much for 40 portions?
1.2 kg ÷ 8 = 0.15 kg per portion; 0.15 × 40 = 6 kg. Another way: 40 ÷ 8 = 5 times the recipe, so 1.2 × 5 = 6 kg.
A pot of soup holds 6 litres. How many 300 ml portions?

blocks.note: Spices, salt and pepper do not always scale in a straight line. For a big batch, add a little less than the sum gives, taste, and add more if needed.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **stock** is a flavoured liquid made by gently simmering bones, vegetables and herbs in water. It is the base of sauces, soups, stews and gravies. A good stock is clear, has a clean flavour and a little body from the gelatine that comes out of the bones.

head: Ingredient
What it gives
Notes
rows: Use fresh, clean bones with some meat on them. Chop big bones so that more flavour comes out. Chicken, beef, fish, goat and pork bones are all used.
Start cold. Use about 2 to 3 litres of water to each kilogram of bones.
Onion, carrot and celery, roughly cut, about one part to ten parts of water by weight. Leek is often added. The vegetables are strained out.
A tied bundle of thyme, bay leaf and parsley stalks (in Jamaica, thyme and scallion are common), so it can be lifted out whole.
Whole, not ground, which would cloud the stock.
For brown stock only, in small amounts.
**No salt**: a stock is often reduced later, and salt would become far too strong.

head: Stock
Bones and flavourings
How it is made
Time (typical)
Used for
rows: Raw bones, blanched first; mirepoix without colour
Cover with cold water, bring slowly to a simmer, skim; no browning
Velouté, cream soups, poached and braised chicken dishes
Bones roasted until brown in a hot oven; mirepoix browned; a little tomato purée
Roast first, then cover with cold water and simmer; skim
Espagnole, brown sauces, gravy, stews, hearty soups
White fish bones and heads, gills removed; onion, celery, parsley, lemon or lime; no oily fish
Sweat in a little butter without colour, cover with cold water, simmer gently
Onion, carrot, celery, leek, herbs, peppercorns; no cabbage or strong vegetables

ul: **Why blanch bones for a white stock?** Boil the bones for a few minutes, drain and rinse them. This removes blood and impurities so that the stock stays clear and white.
**Why roast bones for a brown stock?** Browning gives colour and a deeper, roasted flavour.
**Why only 20 minutes for fish?** Fish bones are thin and give up their flavour fast. Longer simmering makes the stock bitter, cloudy and strongly 'fishy'.
**Why no oily fish?** Oily fish (such as mackerel) give a strong, greasy stock. Use white fish bones, such as snapper.

flow: Prepare the bones (blanch or roast) and cut the vegetables roughly
Put the bones in the stockpot and cover with **cold** water
Bring slowly to the boil, then turn the heat down to a **gentle simmer**
**Skim** off the scum and fat as it rises, using a skimmer and ladle
Add the mirepoix, bouquet garni and peppercorns (fish stock: add them at the start)
Simmer gently, skimming now and then and topping up with hot water if the bones show
Taste to see that the flavour is right
Strain through a fine strainer or muslin, without pressing the bones
Cool fast, cover, label and refrigerate or freeze

head: Rule
Reason
rows: Flavour and protein come out slowly, and the scum rises slowly and can be skimmed off. Hot water seals the surface of the bones and makes the stock cloudy.
Hard boiling breaks fat and bits of bone into the liquid, making it cloudy, greasy and bitter.
Scum and fat make a stock cloudy and give an off taste.
A stock may be reduced, and salt would then be too strong. Salt it only in the finished dish.
Strain through a fine strainer or muslin
Removes small bits and gives a clear stock.
A hot, big pot sits in the danger zone for hours, and bacteria grow fast.

head: Fault
Likely cause
How to prevent it
rows: Boiled hard; not skimmed; stirred; poor-quality bones; pressed on the bones when straining
Simmer gently; skim; do not stir; strain gently through a fine cloth.
Skim often; chill the stock and lift off the set fat.
Too much water; too little time; too few bones
Use the recipe's amounts; reduce the strained stock.
Fish stock simmered too long; burnt bones or vegetables
Fish: 20 to 30 minutes only. Roast to a rich brown, not black.
Left warm too long; badly cooled
Cool fast; never leave it on the stove overnight.

blocks.note: Clean, sound trimmings (onion and carrot ends, celery leaves, herb stalks, chicken carcasses, fish heads and bones) go to the stockpot, not the bin. Never use food that has been on the floor, or that is spoiled.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: Do not rely on a stock 'cooking out' germs after it has been left warm. Some bacteria make poisons that boiling does not destroy. Chill it fast.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Many kitchens use stock cubes, powders and pastes for speed. They are very salty. Taste before you add salt, and follow the maker's amounts. They do not replace a good stock where flavour and body matter, but they are safe, handy and consistent.
A thickener gives a sauce or soup body so that it coats a spoon or holds on a plate. Each one works differently and gives a different finish.

head: Thickener
What it is
How you use it
Finish
rows: Equal weights of fat (butter, margarine or oil) and flour, cooked together.
Melt the fat, stir in the flour and cook it. Add cold or warm liquid a little at a time, stirring. Simmer for at least 10 minutes to cook out the raw flour taste.
Starch mixed with a little cold water or stock.
Stir the slurry into a hot sauce and bring it to the boil, stirring, until it clears. Never add dry starch to hot liquid: it lumps.
Cornflour: slightly cloudy. Arrowroot: clear and glossy, and does not get a starchy taste; do not boil it long.
Equal parts soft butter and flour kneaded into a paste.
Whisk small pieces into a hot sauce at the end to thicken it quickly; simmer a few minutes.
Smooth, slightly glossy. Good for last-minute fixes.
Egg yolks and cream mixed together.
Add a little hot soup to the liaison, then stir it back into the pot **off the boil**. Do not boil it again.
Rich, smooth and creamy. Boiling makes it curdle.
Boiling a liquid so that water steams away.
Simmer uncovered until the sauce has thickened and the flavour is stronger.
Concentrated, glossy, with no added starch.
Cooked vegetables or pulses blended or mashed.
The vegetable itself thickens the soup.
Thick, with the flavour of the main ingredient.

head: Roux
Cooked for (typical)
Colour
Used for
rows: About 2 minutes, until it stops smelling of raw flour; no colour
Béchamel and other white sauces and soups
About 10 minutes or more, on a gentle heat

blocks.p: The longer a roux is cooked, the more colour and flavour it takes on, and the **less thickening power** it has. Do not let a roux burn: if black specks appear, throw it away and start again.

ul: Keep the roux and the liquid at different temperatures: cold liquid into a hot roux, or warm liquid into a cool roux, never both hot at once.
Add the liquid a **little at a time**, stirring all the time, until the mixture is smooth, then add the rest.
Whisk well in the corners of the pan.
If lumps form, **whisk hard** or pass the sauce through a fine strainer. Blending with a stick blender also works.
Never try to fix lumps by adding more flour.

blocks.p: Sauces are made to a consistency to suit their use. A **coating** consistency is thick enough to cover the back of a spoon, and a finger drawn across it leaves a clean line. Thin sauces pour; thick sauces hold their shape and are used in dishes such as croquettes.

blocks.note: A sauce thickens as it cools. If a sauce is for holding, make it a little thinner than you need, or thin it with hot stock or milk.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: Roux is made with wheat flour, so a sauce thickened with it contains **gluten**. Tell guests who cannot eat gluten, or use cornflour or arrowroot.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Classical cookery has five basic sauces, known as the **mother sauces** (or foundation sauces). Hundreds of other sauces are made from them by adding flavourings. If you know the five, you can make most of the sauces on a menu.

head: Mother sauce
Made from
Colour
Typical uses
rows: Milk thickened with a white roux
Macaroni pie, lasagne, creamed vegetables, fish pie
White stock (chicken, veal or fish) thickened with a blond roux
Chicken and fish dishes, cream soups
Brown stock thickened with a brown roux, with browned mirepoix and tomato
Tomatoes cooked with vegetables, herbs and stock
An emulsion of egg yolks and warm butter, with a reduction of vinegar and peppercorns

blocks.p: A medium béchamel uses about 50 to 60 g butter and 50 to 60 g flour to one litre of milk. A thicker sauce uses more roux, a thinner one uses less.

flow: Heat the milk gently (with an onion, a clove and a bay leaf if flavouring it) and strain it
Melt the butter in a heavy saucepan
Stir in the flour and cook for about 2 minutes without colour (a white roux)
Take it off the heat and add the warm milk a little at a time, whisking to a smooth paste
Return to the heat, bring to the boil, stirring, and simmer for about 10 minutes
Season with salt, white pepper and a little grated nutmeg; strain if you need it very smooth

blocks.h: Variations of béchamel, velouté and others

head: Base sauce
Add
Result
Used with
rows: Cream and a liaison of egg yolks

flow: Melt the butter and keep it warm; boil vinegar and crushed peppercorns until reduced to a spoonful, and strain
Whisk the yolks and the reduction in a bowl over a pan of **barely simmering** water, until the mixture is thick and creamy and holds a trail
Take it off the heat
Whisk in the warm butter **a little at a time** so the sauce emulsifies
Season with salt, a little cayenne and lemon or lime juice
Strain if you wish; keep warm in a bain-marie

blocks.p: A typical proportion is about 3 egg yolks to 200 to 250 g of butter. Hollandaise is an **emulsion**: tiny droplets of fat held in the liquid by the lecithin in the yolks.

head: Problem
Cause
Fix
rows: Too hot; or the butter was added too fast; or too much butter
Take it off the heat. Whisk a spoon of warm water into a clean bowl and slowly whisk the split sauce into it, or start with a fresh yolk and whisk the split sauce in.
Yolks not cooked enough, or the butter was too hot
Whisk over gentle heat a little longer.
Over the heat too long, or the water was boiling
Start again: it cannot be saved.

blocks.note: Hollandaise contains lightly cooked egg yolks and is kept warm for service, which makes it a food safety risk (Salmonella). Use fresh, sound eggs from a trusted supplier, or pasteurised yolks if your Centre's plan says so. Make small batches, keep it warm (not hot and not cold) for a short time only, and throw away what is left over.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Sweat chopped onion and garlic in a little oil without colour.
Add tomatoes (fresh, peeled and seeded, or tinned), tomato paste if needed, herbs such as thyme, a bay leaf and stock.
Simmer gently until the sauce is thick and the raw tomato taste is gone, then season. Sieve or blend if a smooth sauce is wanted.
A little sugar can balance the acid in sharp tomatoes.

blocks.p: Espagnole is made from brown stock, a brown roux, browned mirepoix and tomato, simmered for a long time and skimmed. It is the base of rich brown sauces. **Gravy** is the sauce made from the juices left in a roasting tray: pour off the fat, add stock to the tray, scrape up the browned bits, thicken lightly if needed, simmer, season and strain.

ul: Hold hot sauces at about 63 °C or above, as your Centre's food safety plan says, in a bain-marie or on a low heat.
To stop a skin forming, cover the surface with buttered paper or cling film pressed on the sauce, or float a little melted butter on top.
Stir a held sauce now and then, and keep it covered.
Hollandaise is the exception: it is held warm, not hot, and for a short time only.

blocks.p: A soup is a liquid food served hot or cold, made from stock, vegetables, meat, fish, pulses or a mixture. It may be a light start to a meal or a full meal in a bowl.

head: Group
Type
What it is
Examples
rows: A clear, light soup of stock with small pieces of vegetable, meat or grain left in. Not thickened.
Chicken noodle broth; Jamaican chicken soup
A very clear, rich, strongly flavoured stock, cleared with a raft.
Vegetables or pulses cooked and blended. Thickened by the vegetable itself.
Pumpkin, gungo peas, split peas, carrot
A purée or velouté with cream or milk added at the end.
Cream of pumpkin, cream of chicken, cream of mushroom
A velouté sauce thinned with stock.
A thick, chunky soup of fish or seafood, often with potato and milk.
A smooth, rich soup of shellfish.

flow: Make or heat a good, clear stock
Prepare the vegetable garnish (julienne, brunoise or paysanne)
Cook the garnish gently in the stock until just tender
Skim, taste and season
Serve hot, in warm bowls

blocks.h: Making a purée or cream soup

flow: Sweat the chopped onion in a little oil or butter without colour
Add the main vegetable and cook it for a few minutes
Add the stock and simmer until the vegetable is very soft
Blend until smooth, **safely** (see the blender rules)
Return to a clean pan; adjust the thickness with hot stock
Add cream or coconut milk, if used, and reheat gently without boiling
Season, taste and garnish

blocks.p: Consommé is made by clarifying a good stock. A **raft** of lean minced meat, egg white and chopped mirepoix is mixed into the cold stock. As the stock heats slowly, the egg white sets and rises, carrying the cloudy particles with it and forming a raft on top. The soup then simmers gently under the raft for about an hour or more, without stirring. It is then lifted off carefully, and the consommé is strained through muslin.

blocks.note: Consommé is a speciality; know what the raft is and why it works, but expect to do it with your instructor's help.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Let very hot soup cool a little first.
Fill the jug **no more than half or two-thirds** full; hot liquid expands and can push the lid off.
Fit the lid tightly and hold it down with a folded, dry cloth.
Start on the lowest speed, and increase it slowly.
Blend in batches. Never take the lid off a running blender.
A **stick blender** is safer for large pots if it is kept below the surface so that it does not splash.

blocks.p: Soup is a big part of Jamaican food. 'Saturday soup' is a tradition in many homes, and hotels and restaurants serve these soups to guests from Jamaica and abroad. Most are thick, hearty and often a meal in themselves.

head: Soup
Main ingredients
How it is thickened and flavoured
rows: Red kidney beans, salted meat or pigtail, yam, coco, carrot, potato, spinners, thyme, scallion, pimento, whole Scotch bonnet
Beans cooked until soft thicken the soup; some are mashed. Spinners and the starchy provisions add body.
Callaloo, okra, coconut milk, salted meat, yam, coco, thyme, scallion, pimento, whole Scotch bonnet
Callaloo and okra thicken it, coconut milk makes it rich and green.
Fish heads or small whole fish, green banana, pumpkin, thyme, scallion, pimento, hot pepper
A light, strongly flavoured broth, often served in a cup. Strained or served with the vegetables.
Goat head and offal, green banana, yam, pumpkin, thyme, scallion, pimento, Scotch bonnet
A long-simmered, rich, thick soup, often served at celebrations.
Chicken, pumpkin, yam, coco, carrot, potato, spinners, thyme, scallion, pimento
Pumpkin dissolves into the broth and thickens it.
Gungo peas, salted meat, pumpkin, yam, spinners, thyme, coconut milk if used
Pumpkin, carrot, onion, stock, thyme, pimento
Blended (or left in chunks, Jamaican style); cream or coconut milk may be added.

ul: **Spinners:** small, long dumplings made from flour and water (sometimes with a pinch of salt), rolled between the palms into thin 'spindles' and dropped into the soup. Make a firm dough, so that they do not fall apart.

**Whole Scotch bonnet pepper:** added whole, **unburst**, for its flavour and aroma without too much heat. Take it out before serving. If it bursts, the soup is much hotter, and anyone who finds it can be burned.
**Thyme and scallion:** tied or added whole and removed at the end, so no one chokes on a woody stem.
**Pimento (allspice):** whole berries add a warm, spicy flavour.
**Salted pigtail, salted beef:** must be soaked or boiled first to take out extra salt. Taste the soup before you add salt.
**Coconut milk:** adds richness, and the soup must be reheated gently and not boiled hard, which can make it split.

blocks.h: Red kidney beans: a safety rule

blocks.p: Raw and undercooked red kidney beans contain a natural **toxin (phytohaemagglutinin)** that can cause severe vomiting and diarrhoea. The rule is: **soak the beans for at least 5 hours or overnight; throw the soaking water away; boil the beans hard in fresh water for at least 10 minutes; then simmer them until completely soft.** Slow cooking at low temperatures alone is not enough.

ul: Always throw the soaking water away, never cook the beans in it.
Gungo peas, split peas and other dried pulses are cooked in the same careful way and should be soft.
A pressure cooker can be used to cook soaked beans, as the maker says.

blocks.note: Never use canned beans in a recipe that calls for dried ones without changing the recipe: canned beans are already cooked. Raw dried beans must never be added straight to a slow soup.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Sort and wash the beans; soak them overnight; throw away the water
Soak the salted meat or pigtail, and rinse it
Cover the beans with fresh water, boil hard for at least 10 minutes, then simmer until soft, skimming the scum
Add the meat, and the yam, coco, carrot and potato cut in even pieces
Add thyme, scallion, pimento and a whole, unburst Scotch bonnet
Make the spinners from a firm dough and add them near the end
Cook until the provisions and spinners are done; remove the pepper and herb stalks
Taste with a clean spoon, adjust the seasoning, serve hot

blocks.note: In Jamaica, many cooks use a pressure cooker for red peas soup and for tough items such as cow foot and goat. Follow the maker's instructions: never fill past the maximum mark, let the pressure fall fully before opening the lid, and never force it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: **Taste with a clean spoon every time.** Ladle a little into a clean spoon or small dish, taste, and put the used spoon in the wash-up. Never taste from the spoon you are cooking with, and never put the tasting spoon back into the pot.
Season at the **end** of cooking, after any reduction, and in small amounts. You can add salt, but you cannot take it out.
Taste for salt, pepper, acidity (a little lime juice or vinegar can lift a flat sauce), sweetness, and thickness.
Stock cubes, salted meat and some sauces are already salty.

head: Check
What you look for
rows: Hot soups and sauces at about 63 °C or above, checked with a clean probe.
A soup should be thick enough to carry its garnish. A sauce should coat the back of a spoon.
Balanced and seasoned, with no raw flour taste.
Right colour, no skin, scum, grease or lumps.
Clean bowl rim; a garnish that suits the dish.

ul: A garnish adds colour and flavour: a swirl of cream or coconut milk and chopped herbs on a pumpkin soup, a few fine vegetable strips on a broth, a slice of bread or festival with fish tea.
Serve hot soup in **warm** bowls and cold soup in cold bowls. Never serve hot soup in a cold bowl: it loses heat at once.
A soup portion is typically about 200 to 250 ml as a starter, and more as a main course. Use a measured ladle so that every guest gets the same amount.
Wipe the rim of the bowl clean. Do not fill to the brim.

Roux and spinners contain wheat (gluten). Cream, milk, butter and cheese contain milk. Hollandaise and some soups contain eggs. Fish stock and fish soups contain fish; some chowders contain shellfish.
Stock may contain celery, and some stock cubes contain gluten or celery.
A vegetarian guest needs vegetable stock, not chicken or beef stock, and a sauce made without meat or fish.
When in doubt, read the label, ask the chef and never guess.

blocks.note: Never put guests' leftovers back into the pot, and never mix a new batch into an old one.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Cooling, storing, reheating and cleaning up

blocks.p: Hot stock, sauce and soup are warm, wet and full of nutrients, which is exactly what bacteria need. Between about 5 °C and 63 °C (the **danger zone**) they multiply fast. A big pot can stay in the danger zone for many hours. So the way you cool, store and reheat them matters as much as the way you cook them.

flow: Strain the stock, sauce or soup into shallow containers, no more than about 5 cm deep
Stand the containers in an ice bath (a sink of cold water and ice) and stir now and then, or use a blast chiller
Do not put a very hot pot straight into the fridge: it warms the other food
Cover when cool; label with the name, the date and the time
Refrigerate at 5 °C or below, or freeze at -18 °C or below

ul: A common guide is to cool from hot to about 21 °C within 2 hours, and then to 5 °C within a further 4 hours. Your Centre's plan gives the exact limits.
Do not leave a pot to cool on the stove overnight.
Stir a pot in an ice bath so that the middle cools too.
Fat that sets on top of cold stock can be lifted off and thrown away.
Cover and label with the name, date and use-by date. Use clean, covered containers.
Store at 5 °C or below, on a shelf **below ready-to-eat food and above raw meat**.
Use first in, first out. A good guide for stocks and soups is to use them within about 2 to 3 days if refrigerated; follow your Centre's plan.
Freeze extra stock in labelled, dated containers at -18 °C or below.
Thaw in the fridge, not on the counter.

head: Step
Rule
rows: Bring to the boil, or to at least about 74 °C in the centre, checked with a clean probe and recorded. Do it quickly, on the stove or in the oven, never in a bain-marie.
**Once only.** Never cool and reheat the same food again; throw away what is left over.
At about 63 °C or above, in a bain-marie or a hot cupboard. Do not use it to reheat.
Do not keep food hot for hours: quality drops and so does safety. Your plan sets the limit.
Throw away what has been held, served or left on a buffet.

ul: Soak and wash stockpots, saucepans, whisks, ladles and strainers in hot detergent water; rinse and sanitise; dry.
Take blenders apart (after switching off and unplugging) to clean the blade, jug and seal. The blade is very sharp: wash it with a brush, never with your fingers.
Clean stove tops, benches and the floor; mop up grease.
Strain fat and food waste before it goes down the sink, because it blocks drains. Put it in the right bin.
Check the pressure cooker's seal, valve and lid, and clean them as the maker says.
Wash your hands, and put away the clean equipment.
Clean and sanitise anything raw bones touched.
Write the temperatures on the temperature log (cooling, reheating and hot-holding).
Label and date everything you store.
Report faulty equipment, such as a loose pressure cooker seal or a cracked blender jug.

terms: A flavoured liquid made by simmering bones, vegetables and herbs in water.
Roughly cut onion, carrot and celery used to flavour stocks and sauces.
A tied bundle of herbs added for flavour and taken out at the end.
Lifting scum and fat off the surface of a stock or sauce.
To cook in liquid that is just below boiling, with small bubbles.
Boiling a liquid so that water steams away and the flavour gets stronger.
Equal weights of fat and flour cooked together to thicken a sauce.
Starch mixed with cold liquid, to thicken a hot sauce.
A fine white starch that gives a clear, glossy sauce.
Soft butter and flour kneaded together, whisked in at the end to thicken.
Egg yolks and cream used to thicken and enrich a soup or sauce; never boiled.
Tiny droplets of fat held in a liquid, as in hollandaise.
One of five basic sauces from which others are made.
A white sauce of milk thickened with a white roux.
A sauce of white stock thickened with a blond roux.
The classical brown sauce, made with brown stock and brown roux.
An emulsion of egg yolks and butter, flavoured with a reduction.
A sauce made from the juices of roasted meat.
A clear soup cleared of cloudiness by a raft.
The layer of minced meat, egg white and vegetables that clears a consommé.
Food blended or sieved until smooth.
A thick, chunky soup of fish or seafood, usually with potato and milk.
Small, long dumplings added to Jamaican soups.
A pan of hot water used to keep sauces warm.
Thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.
The temperature range, about 5 °C to 63 °C, in which bacteria grow fastest.
Having everything ready before you start to cook.
A written recipe with exact amounts and method, so a dish is the same every time.

c1.title: A cloudy chicken stock at a hotel in Ocho Rios
c1.text: Chef Andrea asks trainee Dwayne to make 20 litres of chicken stock for the next day. He puts the bones in a stockpot of hot water, adds a handful of salt and boils the pot hard for four hours, stirring now and then. The stock comes out cloudy and greasy. Dwayne is tired and the pot is very heavy, so he carries it alone to the walk-in fridge and puts it on the shelf, with the lid on.

c2.title: Sauces at a Sunday brunch in Mandeville
c2.text: At a Sunday brunch in Mandeville, trainee Latoya makes a cheese sauce. She adds all the cold milk to a hot roux at once and finds small lumps. Later she makes hollandaise for 30 poached eggs at 9 a.m. She keeps the whole batch in a bain-marie until the last guest leaves at 1 p.m. Just before service, a second batch looks greasy and starts to separate.

c3.title: Saturday soup for a church group in St. Elizabeth
c3.text: Brother Winston, a volunteer cook, helps trainee Orville make red peas soup for 50 people for a church lunch in St. Elizabeth. They put the dried beans in a pot, cover them with water and cook them on low heat for two hours with salted pigtail. Orville drops the whole Scotch bonnet into the pot, and it bursts when he stirs. Brother Winston wants to speed up the cooking in a pressure cooker and open the lid straight away when the heat is turned off.

c4.title: Pumpkin soup for a villa wedding in Port Antonio
c4.text: A villa in Port Antonio is serving cream of pumpkin soup to 40 guests at a wedding. The recipe for 8 portions uses 1.2 kg of pumpkin and 1.6 litres of stock. Trainee Shelly cooks the soup, then pours it, still boiling, into a jug blender filled to the top, and switches it to the highest speed. After service she has 6 litres left over and wants to keep it for tomorrow.

c5.title: A fish tea and a fish sauce for the guesthouse in Treasure Beach
c5.text: Chef Collin asks trainee Keisha to make a fish stock for fish tea and a velouté-based fish sauce for the evening. Keisha uses snapper heads and bones, with the gills still on, and simmers the stock for three hours while she works on other jobs. A guest is allergic to wheat and has ordered the fish with sauce.

questions.q: Which two things most likely made Dwayne's stock cloudy and greasy?
o: Hard boiling and stirring, which broke fat into the liquid
The hot start and the salt, which pulled the fat out of the bones
Four hours of cooking and the lid on the pot overnight
Too much water and too few vegetables in the pot
questions.why: A hard boil and stirring break fat and tiny particles into the stock, making it cloudy and greasy. Stock should start with cold water, simmer gently, be skimmed and not be stirred.

questions.q: Why did Chef Andrea tell Dwayne not to add salt?
o: Salt stops the bones from giving up their flavour
Salt makes the stock cloudy and the scum harder to skim
The stock may be reduced later and would become too salty
Salt is taken out by the strainer at the end
questions.why: Stock is often reduced when it is made into sauces or soups, which concentrates any salt. Season the finished dish, not the stock.

questions.q: What should Dwayne have done with a full 20-litre pot instead of carrying it alone?
o: Asked for help, or ladled some of it into smaller containers first
Carried it with wet cloths so it could be lifted with less effort
Slid it along the floor to the fridge so that it did not splash
Carried it quickly so that the stock was in the cold sooner
questions.why: A full stockpot is heavy and can scald and injure the back. Reduce the load or get a second person. Dry, not wet, cloths should be used for hot pots.

questions.q: Dwayne put the whole pot of hot stock on a shelf in the fridge. What is the main problem?
o: The lid will trap the steam and make the stock taste flat
The stock will take hours to cool, and will warm the food around it
The fridge will freeze the stock around the edges first
The fat will set on top and cannot be skimmed off later
questions.why: A large, deep pot of hot stock cools slowly in the middle, staying in the danger zone while bacteria grow, and it warms other food in the fridge. Strain it into shallow containers and chill it in an ice bath.

questions.q: What caused the lumps in Latoya's cheese sauce?
o: The cheese was added before the milk had started to thicken
The roux was cooked too long and became too dry to mix
A cold liquid was poured into the hot roux all at once
The milk was too fresh and the flour too finely ground
questions.why: Adding all the liquid at once makes the flour clump before it can spread. Add the milk gradually, whisking until smooth at each stage; whisk hard or strain if lumps still form.

questions.q: Which is the best way to rescue a sauce that has a few small lumps?
o: Stir in more flour so that the lumps are absorbed
Whisk it hard, or pass it through a fine strainer
Cook it until the lumps break down by themselves
Pour in cold water and boil it fast until it clears
questions.why: Hard whisking or a fine strainer removes lumps. More flour only makes more lumps, and boiling does not break them down.

questions.q: The hollandaise was held in the bain-marie from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. What should Latoya have done instead?
o: Kept it hot, at above 80 °C, so no germs could grow
Made small batches, kept them warm briefly and thrown away leftovers
Made it all at once, and chilled it, then reheated it each time
Made it at room temperature on the bench for the whole morning
questions.why: Hollandaise contains lightly cooked egg yolk, so it is made in small batches and held warm for a short time only. Too hot splits it, and too long risks bacteria. Leftovers go in the bin.

questions.q: The second hollandaise batch looks greasy and starts to split. What is the best first action?
o: Take it off the heat and whisk it into a spoon of warm water
Turn up the heat so that the sauce comes together faster
Add more melted butter so that the sauce is thicker
Strain it and use it as a thin dressing without whisking
questions.why: A split hollandaise is rescued by taking it off the heat and slowly whisking it into a little warm water or a fresh yolk to re-form the emulsion. More heat or butter makes it worse.

questions.q: What is wrong with the way the red beans were cooked?
o: They were boiled too hard, which spoiled the colour of the soup
They were cooked without soaking, so they were too hard to eat
They were not boiled hard in fresh water, so a toxin may be left
They were cooked in salted water, which made the skins hard
questions.why: Raw red kidney beans contain a toxin. Soak them, throw the soaking water away, boil them hard in fresh water for at least 10 minutes and then simmer them until soft. Low heat alone may not destroy the toxin.

questions.q: The Scotch bonnet burst when Orville stirred. What is the likely effect on the soup?
o: The soup will be thicker, because the seeds act as a thickener
The soup will be much hotter, and may burn anyone who eats it
The soup will be milder, since the flesh dissolves in the liquid
The soup will turn red, since the skin gives off its colour
questions.why: A whole pepper gives aroma and mild heat. Once it bursts, the seeds and membrane release strong heat. Taste carefully, and tell the chef; the soup may need more liquid or to be started again for sensitive guests.

questions.q: What should happen when Brother Winston uses the pressure cooker?
o: Fill the pot to the top, so that nothing burns on the bottom
Open the lid as soon as the heat is off, to save time
Follow the maker's guide, and open the lid once the pressure has dropped
Block the valve with a cloth so that the pressure builds faster
questions.why: Opening a pressure cooker too early, overfilling it or blocking the valve can cause a violent release of steam. Follow the maker's instructions and wait until the pressure has dropped fully.

questions.q: Salted pigtail goes into the soup. What should be done about the salt before serving?
o: Soak or boil the pigtail first, and taste before adding any salt
Add extra water at the end to wash the salt out of the soup
Add the salt at the start, so that it has time to dissolve
Skim the salt from the top of the soup with the scum
questions.why: Salted meat is very salty. Soaking or boiling it removes some salt, and tasting before seasoning stops the soup being over-salted. Salt cannot be skimmed off.

questions.q: How much pumpkin does Shelly need for 40 portions of the soup?
o: 5 kg
4 kg
6 kg
7.5 kg
questions.why: 40 ÷ 8 = 5 times the recipe, so 1.2 kg × 5 = 6 kg. Check it another way: 1.2 ÷ 8 = 0.15 kg per portion, and 0.15 × 40 = 6 kg.

questions.q: Shelly filled the jug to the top with boiling soup. What is the danger?
o: The jug may crack from the heat before it starts to turn
The soup may be blended too finely and lose its flavour
The blades may blunt as they pass through the hot liquid
Hot soup can push the lid off and spray out, causing scalds
questions.why: Hot liquid expands and, with the speed of the blades, can force the lid off. Cool the soup a little, fill the jug only part way, hold the lid down with a folded cloth, start slowly or use a stick blender.

questions.q: What is the best way to deal with the 6 litres of soup left after service?
o: Leave it in the covered pot on the stove to cool, then chill it in the morning
Put the whole pot in the fridge while it is hot, with the lid on tightly
Chill it in shallow containers in an ice bath, then cover and label it
Keep it warm in a bain-marie overnight so it is ready for lunch
questions.why: Shallow containers in an ice bath get soup through the danger zone fast. Leaving it warm overnight or chilling a big hot pot lets bacteria grow.

questions.q: Why is a three-hour simmer a mistake for Keisha's fish stock?
o: Fish bones go hard if simmered too long and the stock cannot be strained
Fish stock needs a much higher heat, which makes it cook more quickly
Fish stock goes bitter and cloudy if it is simmered for too long
A long simmer takes all of the salt out of the fish bones
questions.why: Fish bones give up flavour in 20 to 30 minutes. A longer time makes the stock bitter and cloudy.

questions.q: What should Keisha do with the gills on the fish heads?
o: Leave them in, because they add colour to the stock
Take them out before cooking, because they make the stock bitter
Chop them small so they do not show in the finished stock
Boil them separately and add the water to the stock
questions.why: Gills spoil quickly and give a bitter taste and cloudy appearance. Remove them, along with any blood, before making fish stock.

questions.q: The wheat-allergic guest has ordered fish with a velouté-based sauce. What should the kitchen do?
o: Serve the sauce as usual, since the roux cooks out the wheat
Make a sauce thickened with cornflour or arrowroot, and tell the chef
Scrape the sauce off the fish before it is served
Tell the guest to ask the waiter to take the sauce off the plate
questions.why: A roux is made with wheat flour, so a velouté contains gluten. A starch thickener such as cornflour or arrowroot can replace it, with clean equipment, and the chef must know.

questions.q: A cook adds cornflour to a pot of hot sauce by sprinkling it straight in. What happens?
o: It lumps, because the starch must be mixed with cold liquid first
It thickens at once and gives a perfectly smooth, glossy finish
It sinks to the bottom and burns, because starch is heavier than the sauce
It turns the sauce clear, because starch removes the colour
questions.why: Dry starch dropped into hot liquid swells on the outside and forms lumps. Mix it with a little cold water first (a slurry), then stir it in and bring it to the boil.

questions.q: Which mother sauce is made from white stock and a blond roux?
o: Velouté
Béchamel
Espagnole
Hollandaise
questions.why: Velouté is white stock thickened with a blond roux. Béchamel is milk with a white roux, espagnole is brown stock with a brown roux, and hollandaise is egg yolk and butter.
